definitions.definition: Set of electronic circuits on a small chip of semiconductor material, typically silicon, containing transistors, resistors and capacitors.
Design of circuits that process continuous signals, focused on amplification, filtering, modulation and voltage regulation.
Minimum gate-to-source voltage required to create a conductive channel between the source and drain terminals of a field-effect transistor.
Resistance between the drain and source terminals of a MOSFET when it is turned on, set in ohms.
Small leakage current flowing between the drain and source terminals of a FET when the gate-to-source voltage is zero.
Small current flowing between the gate and source terminals of a MOSFET when a specified voltage is applied between them.
Maximum voltage that can be applied between drain and source, with the gate shorted to the source, without damaging avalanche breakdown.
Capacitance between the gate and source terminals with the drain shorted to the source, made up of gate-source and gate-drain capacitances.
Capacitance between the gate and drain terminals of a MOSFET, also called feedback or Miller capacitance, which affects switching speed.
Parasitic capacitance measured across the drain-source terminals of a MOSFET in the off state, which affects switching speed.
Cutoff, linear (triode) and saturation, set by the gate-to-source and drain-to-source voltages relative to the threshold voltage.
Three-terminal device with gate, drain and source terminals, used to control current.
Transistor used as a resistor in the triode region, giving compact on-chip area and electronically controllable resistance.
Two-terminal component whose current at any instant of time is independent of the voltage across it.
Circuit in which two matched transistors share the same gate-to-source voltage, so the output current is a copy of the input current.
Transistor operated as a switch, off in cutoff with negligible drain current and on in the triode region.
Circuit that amplifies the difference between two input signals and is immune to external noise and interference.
Parameter representing channel-length modulation, showing how drain current rises slightly with drain-to-source voltage even in saturation.
Part of a differential amplifier, across which the output is taken, that defines gain, bandwidth, output common-mode range and supply rejection.
Configuration that raises the output resistance of a common-source amplifier in order to achieve higher intrinsic gain.
Voltage gain of a transistor stage given by the product of its transconductance and its output resistance.
Ratio of the change in output voltage to the change in differential input voltage of an op-amp.
Frequency range over which an amplifier can operate effectively.
Product of open-loop gain and bandwidth, which stays approximately constant as gain falls after the dominant pole.
Ability of an op-amp to reject signals common to both inputs, given by the ratio of differential gain to common-mode gain.
Measure of how well an op-amp rejects variations or noise in the supply voltage, as a ratio of differential gain to supply-noise gain.
Range of input voltages over which an op-amp operates correctly without distortion.
Maximum positive and negative output levels reachable before the output transistor enters saturation.
Noise component of a CMOS op-amp that is proportional to channel resistance.
Low-frequency noise, also called 1/f noise, that dominates at low frequencies and is higher in MOSFETs.
Cascade of amplifier stages that achieves higher gain and better impedance matching than one stage, with a high-impedance input and low-impedance output.
Operational amplifier made of a differential input stage followed by a common-source gain stage.
Time taken for the output to settle within 0.1% or 1% of its final value after a step input.
Structure equivalent to a planar capacitor with one electrode replaced by a semiconductor, forming the heart of the MOSFET.
Carrier-free region of immobile, negatively charged acceptor ions left when a positive gate voltage pushes holes away from the interface.
Surface layer in which a p-type body flips to n-type, with electrons as majority carriers, once the gate voltage is high enough.
Insulator lying directly below the gate electrode and above the channel, separating the gate from the channel.
Amount by which the gate-to-source voltage exceeds the threshold value.
Representation of an integrated circuit in terms of planar geometric shapes that correspond to the material layers forming its components.
Shortening of the inverted channel region as drain bias increases, which raises saturation drain current and sets the MOSFET output resistance.
Current between source and drain of a MOSFET when the gate voltage is below the threshold voltage.
Log-linear slope of drain current against gate voltage in the subthreshold region, used as a figure of merit for switching efficiency.
Another name for the subthreshold operating region, which is an efficient region for analog micropower design.
Range of voltages over which a current mirror works, bounded by its compliance voltage.
Resistor in a transistor's source that can offset threshold variation in a mirror but lowers its output resistance.
Voltage reference circuit widely used in integrated circuits that gives a nearly constant output tied to the band gap, varying little with supply, load, time or temperature.
Quantity generated from the voltage difference between two p-n junctions at different current densities, rising in proportion to absolute temperature.
Voltage across a diode held at constant current, which falls as temperature rises at about −2 mV per kelvin.
Multi-transistor current source that stacks transistors to give higher output resistance than a single mirror.
Two-stage amplifier, a common-source stage feeding a common-gate stage in FETs, giving very large output resistance.
Increase in the equivalent input capacitance of an inverting voltage amplifier caused by the capacitance between its input and output.
Technique used when a gain stage also serves as a high-impedance output, to counter the effect of feedback capacitance on performance.
Resistance at the drain set by channel length modulation, infinite when the modulation parameter is zero.
DC-coupled electronic amplifier with a differential input, a single-ended output and very high gain.
Voltage required across the input terminals of an op-amp to drive its output voltage to zero, arising from imperfections in the input stage.
Maximum rate at which an output voltage can change, usually specified in volts per microsecond.
Method of stabilising feedback circuits that increases the gain or phase margin, using external parts or an internal dominant pole.
Small current that flows into the inputs of an op-amp because of biasing requirements or leakage.
Device that compares two voltages or currents and outputs a digital signal indicating which is larger.
Comparator built from an amplifier without feedback, which heavily amplifies the input difference so its output saturates high or low.
Use of two switching points, one for rising and one for falling input voltages, whose gap is the trip-point difference.
Clocked, dynamic comparator that uses strong positive feedback during a regeneration phase while the clock is high and resets when it is low.
Comparator that accepts any differential voltage within the power-supply range.
Time a comparator takes to respond, ranging from tens of microseconds for op-amps used as comparators down to a few nanoseconds.
